patch.objective: Identify the brain regions involved in movement (primary motor and somatosensory cortex, basal nuclei, cerebellum, brainstem) and what each contributes
secondaryObjectives: Trace the corticospinal tract and the dorsal column and spinothalamic pathways, including where each crosses the midline

sources.cite: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 16.5 The Coordination and Gait Exams
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 through a summarizing fetch: the cerebellum 'compares motor commands and sensory feedback to generate a new output'; its midline regions compare 'visual information, equilibrium, and proprioceptive feedback to maintain balance'; vestibular signals reach it through the inferior cerebellar peduncle; the brain stem's peduncles connect it to the rest of the brain; in the Romberg test 'Any changes in posture would be the result of proprioceptive deficits'. The case's central signs point to the brainstem and cerebellum, not the inner ear.

sources.cite: CAPTE, Standards and Required Elements for Accreditation of Physical Therapist Education Programs (2024 standards)
sources.note: Relayed from the REQ-232 DPT cases (the course seed's reading of 2026-10-08), not re-read: screening and determining when a patient needs referral to another professional are required elements.
The objective and secondary objectives are the course's own titles.

sources.cite: Edlow JA, Carpenter C, Akhter M, et al. Guidelines for reasonable and appropriate care in the emergency department 3 (GRACE-3): Acute dizziness and vertigo in the emergency department. Acad Emerg Med. 2023;30(5):442-486
sources.note: Read 2026-11-14 through the indexed abstract only (summarizing fetch): for acute dizziness under two weeks, HINTS by trained clinicians in patients with nystagmus; without nystagmus, the severity of gait unsteadiness helps tell central from peripheral causes; CT is not used for acute vestibular syndrome; MRI confirms central or equivocal HINTS findings. The full text was not read.

sources.cite: Hall CD, Herdman SJ, Whitney SL, et al. Vestibular rehabilitation for peripheral vestibular hypofunction: an updated clinical practice guideline from the Academy of Neurologic Physical Therapy of the APTA. J Neurol Phys Ther. 2022;46(2):118-177
sources.note: Read 2026-11-14 (first part of the guideline PDF, summarizing fetch with quotes): gaze stabilization 3 times a day for at least 12 minutes daily in acute or subacute unilateral hypofunction; the guideline 'may not apply to individuals with central vestibular disorders'; stopping when goals are met, symptoms resolve or progress plateaus. Journal and year are from the published citation, not from the fetched excerpt.

sources.cite: NASEMSO National Model EMS Clinical Guidelines, Version 3.0 (rev. March 2022): Suspected Stroke/Transient Ischemic Attack
sources.note: Relayed from the REQ-241 EMT stroke case (read 2026-11-11 in full text, the Iowa HHS copy), not re-read: 'last known well' made specific; early hospital notification; destinations per the local stroke plan; last known well under 24 hours with a positive severity scale may be eligible for thrombectomy.
